steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper asking whether CLIP's generalization on out-of-distribution benchmarks mainly comes from training images that are very similar to the test sets. Motivate the question with foundation models and web-scale data, then list our contributions section by section.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Foundation models, web-scale data, CLIP and its OOD performance
2. Open question: what in the training distribution drives performance; OOD benchmarks may not be OOD for LAION-400M
3. Research question
4. Contributions (Sec. 4.1-4.4, Sec. 5, curated subset)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Foundation models + CLIP
- large models GPT-4, CLIP, LLaMa changing technological + academic landscape; unprecedented performance, breadth of applications
- Foundation Models trained on hundreds of millions or billions of data points scraped from internet
- e.g. OpenCLIP (open-source CLIP) trained on LAION-400M, web-scale, wide variety of image-text pairs
- CLIP backbone of generative models like DALL-E2; remarkable zero-shot + few-shot performance on many tasks, esp. OOD benchmarks ImageNet-Sketch, ImageNet-R, etc.

2. Open question
- prior work: CLIP's performance mainly from its data distribution
- unclear which properties drive it: scale, diversity, density, relation to test set
- OOD benchmarks designed with reference to ImageNet-1k (primary dataset for machine vision progress for several years before web-scale datasets)
- considered OOD: same content (classes) as ImageNet-1k but different style, pose, scale, background, viewpoint
- no guarantee they are dissimilar to LAION-400M
- Fig. 1: samples from ImageNet-Sketch, ImageNet-R; nearest perceptual neighbors in LAION-400M and ImageNet-Train
- LAION-400M: highly similar neighbors, even exact duplicates; ImageNet-Train neighbors relatively dissimilar
- -> models trained on LAION-400M may do well on OOD benchmarks just from semantically + stylistically similar training data

3. Question
- Does CLIP's accuracy on OOD benchmarks mainly stem from highly similar images in its train set?
- highly similar = stylistically + semantically more similar to test sets than any image in ImageNet-1k

4. Contributions
- Sec. 4.1: perceptual similarity; previously shown to capture stylistic + semantic similarity
- Sec. 4.2: nearest-neighbor similarity impacts CLIP performance: (i) high correlation zero-shot accuracy vs nearest-neighbor similarity of test samples; (ii) similarity-based pruning of training set greatly affects performance
- Sec. 4.3: distributions of nearest-neighbor similarities differ substantially across training sets; hypothesis: performance explained by samples causing the difference = highly similar images
- Sec. 4.4: formalize via similarity gap of two training distributions; highly similar images of LAION-400M lie within similarity gap of ImageNet-Train to a test set; pruning aligns the gap so test sets as dissimilar to pruned LAION-400M splits as to ImageNet-Train
- Sec. 5 (central result): training on curated subsets only marginally decreases OOD performance (Tab. 1), surprising; high train-test similarity cannot fully explain performance; other properties of LAION-400M matter
- 100M subset of LAION-400M (¼ original size) where CLIP keeps full OOD performance (Sec. 4.2 & B.4), for future research

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large models like GPT-4, CLIP, or LLaMa are changing the technological and academic landscape because of their unprecedented performance and the wide range of applications they can be used for. A core characteristic of these Foundation Models is that they are trained on hundreds of millions or even billions of data points that are scraped from the internet. For example, OpenCLIP, which is the open-source version of CLIP, is trained on LAION-400M, which is a web-scale dataset with a wide variety of image-text pairs. CLIP is the backbone of generative models like DALL-E2 and it is known for its remarkable zero-shot and few-shot performance on a lot of tasks, especially on out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks like ImageNet-Sketch, ImageNet-R, etc.

Prior work has shown that CLIP's great performance mainly comes from its data distribution. But it is still unclear which specific properties of the training distribution drive the performance, for example its scale, diversity, density, or relation to the test set. OOD benchmarks like ImageNet-Sketch and ImageNet-R were originally designed with reference to ImageNet-1k, which was the primary dataset driving progress in machine vision for several years before web-scale datasets came along. ImageNet-Sketch, ImageNet-R, and others are considered OOD because they have the same content (i.e., classes) as ImageNet-1k but they are different in style, pose, scale, background, or viewpoint. But there is no guarantee that these datasets are also dissimilar to LAION-400M. We show evidence of this in Fig. 1, where we take samples from ImageNet-Sketch and ImageNet-R and look at their nearest perceptual neighbors in LAION-400M and in ImageNet-Train. In LAION-400M we find highly similar neighbors and even exact duplicates, while the neighbors in ImageNet-Train are relatively dissimilar. So models trained on LAION-400M might do well on conventional OOD benchmarks just because they were trained on data points that are semantically and stylistically similar. This leads to the question:

Does CLIP's accuracy on OOD benchmarks mainly stem from highly similar images in its train set?

With highly similar images we mean images that are stylistically and semantically more similar to the test sets than any image in ImageNet-1k is. To answer this question, we make the following contributions:

- In Sec. 4.1 we first introduce perceptual similarity, which has been shown before to capture stylistic and semantic similarity between images. In Sec. 4.2 we show that the similarity of nearest neighbors under this metric generally affects CLIP's performance. Specifically, we (i) see a high correlation between zero-shot accuracy and the nearest-neighbor similarity of test samples and (ii) show that pruning the training set based on similarity greatly affects CLIP's performance.

- Sec. 4.3: nearest-neighbor similarity distributions of training sets differ substantially -> hypothesis: highly similar images explain performance
- Sec. 4.4: formalize highly similar images via similarity gap; LAION-400M images within ImageNet-Train's gap to test set; pruning aligns the gaps
- Sec. 5: training on curated subsets only marginally lowers OOD performance (Tab. 1) -> other properties of LAION-400M matter
- release 100M subset (¼ size) keeping full OOD performance (Sec. 4.2 & B.4)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large models like GPT-4, CLIP, or LLaMa are changing the technological and academic landscape because of their unprecedented performance and the wide range of applications they can be used for. CLIP is the backbone of generative models like DALL-E2 and it is known for its remarkable zero-shot and few-shot performance on a lot of tasks, especially on out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks like ImageNet-Sketch, ImageNet-R, etc.

Prior work has shown that CLIP's great performance mainly comes from its data distribution. But it is still unclear which specific properties of the training distribution drive the performance, for example its scale, diversity, density, or relation to the test set. OOD benchmarks like ImageNet-Sketch and ImageNet-R were originally designed with reference to ImageNet-1k, which was the primary dataset driving progress in machine vision for several years before web-scale datasets came along. ImageNet-Sketch, ImageNet-R, and others are considered OOD because they have the same content (i.e., classes) as ImageNet-1k but they are different in style, pose, scale, background, or viewpoint. But there is no guarantee that these datasets are also dissimilar to LAION-400M. We show evidence of this in Fig. 1, where we take samples from ImageNet-Sketch and ImageNet-R and look at their nearest perceptual neighbors in LAION-400M and in ImageNet-Train. In LAION-400M we find highly similar neighbors and even exact duplicates, while the neighbors in ImageNet-Train are relatively dissimilar. So models trained on LAION-400M might do well on conventional OOD benchmarks just because they were trained on data points that are semantically and stylistically similar. This leads to the question:

Does CLIP's accuracy on OOD benchmarks mainly stem from highly similar images in its train set?

With highly similar images we mean images that are stylistically and semantically more similar to the test sets than any image in ImageNet-1k is. To answer this question, we make the following contributions:

- In Sec. 4.1 we first introduce perceptual similarity, which has been shown before to capture stylistic and semantic similarity between images. In Sec. 4.2 we show that the similarity of nearest neighbors under this metric generally affects CLIP's performance. Specifically, we (i) see a high correlation between zero-shot accuracy and the nearest-neighbor similarity of test samples and (ii) show that pruning the training set based on similarity greatly affects CLIP's performance.

- Based on this, in Sec. 4.3 we compare the distribution of nearest-neighbor similarities of different training sets and find that they are substantially different. Our hypothesis is that CLIP's high performance might be largely explained by the training samples that cause this difference, which we call highly similar images.

- Sec. 4.4 formalizes the notion of highly similar images using the similarity gap of two training distributions. With this formalization, highly similar images of LAION-400M lie within the similarity gap of ImageNet-Train to a given test set, i.e., they are more similar to test samples than any image in ImageNet-Train is. Then we show how pruning can align the similarity gap of both distributions, so that test sets are as dissimilar to pruned LAION-400M-splits as they are to ImageNet-Train.

- Our central result in Sec. 5 is surprising: training CLIP on the curated subsets only decreases performance on the corresponding OOD benchmarks a little bit (Tab. 1). We conclude that high train-test similarity cannot fully explain CLIP's remarkable performance, and other properties of LAION-400M must play a role.

- To help future research into the impact of training on the performance of vision-language foundation models, we curate a 100M subset of LAION-400M (¼ of its original size) where CLIP keeps its full OOD benchmark performance (Sec. 4.2 & B.4).
